CausalChain: Chronic ethanol exposure -> Impairment of hepatocellular autophagy -> Accumulation of p62 -> Enhanced sequestration of Keap1 -> Sustained activation of Nrf2 -> Upregulation of antioxidant and anabolic genes (redirecting glucose and glutamine flux) -> Increased lipogenesis and cellular proliferation -> Elevated risk for progression from ALD to liver cancer (HCC)
Hypothesis: Chronic alcohol exposure impairs autophagy in hepatocytes leading to p62 accumulation, which in turn sequesters Keap1 and causes sustained Nrf2 activation. While this activation initially mitigates oxidative damage, its chronic persistence instigates an anabolic reprogramming that promotes lipogenesis and proliferation, thereby facilitating the progression from alcoholic liver disease to hepatocellular carcinoma.
Abstract: Recent studies have highlighted the dual role of the Keap1-Nrf2 pathway in hepatoprotection and tumorigenesis. While transient Nrf2 activation confers resistance to oxidative damage in diverse liver injuries such as alcoholic liver disease (ALD), chronic stimulation may inadvertently trigger metabolic reprogramming. Our proposed hypothesis suggests that under conditions of chronic ethanol exposure, impaired autophagy leads to p62 accumulation that sequesters Keap1, resulting in sustained Nrf2 activation. This prolonged up‐regulation of Nrf2, although initially protective, re‐directs cellular metabolism towards anabolic pathways, enhancing lipogenesis and promoting cell proliferation. The integrated mechanism may thus serve as a molecular link between chronic alcohol exposure and the progression from liver injury to hepatocellular carcinoma. This hypothesis is testable through in vivo models of chronic alcohol exposure and analysis of autophagy markers, p62 levels, and Nrf2‐dependent metabolic alterations.
